s: D. State taxation of interstate commerce.
States may tax interstate commerce, but not in ways that discriminate against it or tax more than a fair share.

Due process separately requires some minimum connection between the state and the person, property or transaction taxed, and a rational relationship between income attributed to the state and values connected with it (Quill; North Carolina Dept. of Revenue v. Kaestner Trust, 2019).
The Commerce Clause protects the national market; due process protects fairness to the taxpayer.
The intergovernmental immunity doctrine (McCulloch) bars states from taxing the United States directly or discriminating against those who deal with it.
